He died in Rome on 14 July 1614. Beatified in 1742 and canonized in 1746, he was later named, with St. John of God, patron of the sick and of hospitals, and patron of nurses and of the Red Cross tradition of mercy to the wounded.

events.title: The storming of the Bastille
events.shortBlurb: The fall of the Paris fortress opened the French Revolution and a long ordeal for the Church…
body: On the fourteenth of July 1789 a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, the royal fortress and prison that had come to symbolize the old regime. The event is remembered as the opening of the French Revolution, which within a few years overturned the monarchy and the established order of France.

For the Church the Revolution brought the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, the confiscation of ecclesiastical property, the suppression of religious orders, and, in the Reign of Terror, the persecution and execution of priests, religious, and lay faithful who would not conform. It marked the beginning of one of the gravest trials the Church in France had known.

events.title: Keble’s “National Apostasy” sermon begins the Oxford Movement
events.shortBlurb: John Keble mounted the pulpit of the University Church at Oxford and preached against the State’s meddling in the Church — the sermon John Henry Newman would later date as the true start of the movement that led many toward Rome…
body: On 14 July 1833 John Keble preached the Assize Sermon, “National Apostasy,” at St. Mary’s, the University Church of Oxford, protesting the British government’s suppression of Irish bishoprics as an intrusion upon the divine constitution of the Church.

John Henry Newman afterward reckoned this sermon the beginning of the Oxford Movement, which sought to recover the Catholic heritage of the English Church. Its studies of antiquity led Newman and many others, over the following years, into full communion with the Catholic Church.

events.title: The First Crusade captures Jerusalem
events.shortBlurb: After a long march and siege, the armies of the First Crusade breached the walls and took the Holy City, ending the expedition summoned four years earlier at Clermont…
body: On the fifteenth of July 1099, after a siege of some weeks amid great hardship and thirst, the knights of the First Crusade broke into Jerusalem and took the city, the goal of their long march from Europe. The capture fulfilled the aim proclaimed by Pope Urban II at Clermont four years before.

The victory was followed by a terrible slaughter of the city's inhabitants, a stain long remembered. A Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem was established, with Godfrey of Bouillon as its first ruler, opening nearly two centuries of Crusader presence in the Holy Land.

events.title: The death of St. Bonaventure at Lyons
events.shortBlurb: The Seraphic Doctor died during the Second Council of Lyons he had helped to guide…
body: St. Bonaventure, Minister General of the Franciscans and cardinal-bishop of Albano, was one of the chief architects of the Second Council of Lyons, called to seek reunion between the Latin and Greek Churches and reform of Christian life. He preached and labored tirelessly in its sessions.

Worn out by his exertions, he died on the fifteenth of July 1274 while the council was still in session, and was buried at Lyons with the assembled fathers in attendance. The council achieved a short-lived union with the Greeks that did not endure.

events.title: The East-West Schism
events.shortBlurb: Papal legates laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, hardening the breach of East and West…
body: Long-growing tensions between the Latin West and the Greek East — over authority, custom, and points of doctrine — came to a head in 1054, when Pope St. Leo IX sent legates led by Cardinal Humbert to Constantinople to treat with the Patriarch Michael Cerularius. The mission failed amid mutual mistrust.

On the sixteenth of July 1054 the legates laid a bull of excommunication against the patriarch upon the altar of the great church of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch in turn condemned them. Though at the time it seemed one quarrel among many, the day is conventionally reckoned the beginning of the enduring schism between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches; the mutual excommunications were lifted only in 1965.

events.title: The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
events.shortBlurb: The united Christian kings of Spain broke the power of the Almohads in the Reconquista's great turning point…
body: On the sixteenth of July 1212 the combined armies of Castile, Aragon, and Navarre, under King Alfonso VIII of Castile and blessed as a crusade, met the great host of the Almohad Caliphate at Las Navas de Tolosa in the Sierra Morena. After breaking through the enemy lines, the Christians won an overwhelming victory.

The battle shattered Almohad power in the Iberian Peninsula and proved a decisive turning point in the long Reconquista, opening the south of Spain to the advance of the Christian kingdoms in the decades that followed.

events.title: The Scillitan Martyrs
events.shortBlurb: Twelve African Christians were beheaded at Carthage in the earliest dated record of the Latin Church…
body: On the seventeenth of July in the year 180, twelve Christians from the town of Scillium in Roman North Africa were brought before the proconsul Vigellius Saturninus at Carthage. Asked to swear by the genius of the emperor and abandon their faith, they refused; their spokesman Speratus declared simply that he knew only the Lord, the King of kings.

They were condemned and beheaded. The brief account of their trial, the “Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs,” is the earliest precisely dated document of the Church in Latin, a witness to the courage of ordinary believers at the frontiers of the Roman world.

events.title: The Carmelites of Compiègne go to the guillotine
events.shortBlurb: Sixteen Carmelite nuns were executed in Paris, singing as they mounted the scaffold…
body: In the summer of 1794, during the Reign of Terror, sixteen Discalced Carmelite nuns of Compiègne were condemned for continuing their religious life and for “fanaticism” under the revolutionary tribunal. They had offered themselves to God as a sacrifice for the peace of France and the Church.

On the seventeenth of July they were carried to the Place du Trône-Renversé in Paris and guillotined one by one, renewing their vows and singing hymns to the last, the prioress dying last of all. Ten days later Robespierre fell and the Terror ended; the martyrs were beatified in 1906 and canonized in 2024.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Martyrs of Compiègne (vatican.va)

events.title: The First Vatican Council defines papal infallibility
events.shortBlurb: The council solemnly defined the infallibility of the pope in the constitution Pastor Aeternus…
body: The First Vatican Council, convened by Pope Pius IX in 1869, took up the questions of faith and reason and the authority of the Roman Pontiff. After long debate, on the eighteenth of July 1870 it promulgated the dogmatic constitution Pastor Aeternus, defining the primacy of the pope and, under carefully stated conditions, his infallibility when he defines a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church.

The definition was approved by a large majority of the fathers present. The very next day the Franco-Prussian War broke out, and within weeks the seizure of Rome forced the council to be suspended before it could complete its work.

events.title: The suppression of the Society of Jesus
events.shortBlurb: Pope Clement XIV suppressed the Jesuits under pressure from the Catholic courts of Europe…
body: Under sustained pressure from the Bourbon courts of France, Spain, Portugal, and Naples, which had already expelled the Jesuits from their lands, Pope Clement XIV issued on the twenty-first of July 1773 the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, suppressing the Society of Jesus throughout the Church. The order, then numbering some twenty-three thousand members, was dissolved and its works handed over to others.

In parts of Prussia and Russia the Society survived where the brief was not promulgated, preserving a thread of continuity. Pope Pius VII restored the Society of Jesus to the universal Church in 1814.

events.title: The death of St. Bridget of Sweden
events.shortBlurb: The Swedish mystic and foundress died at Rome after years of labor for the Church…
body: St. Bridget of Sweden spent the last decades of her life at Rome, where she pressed for the reform of the clergy and the return of the popes from Avignon, cared for the poor and pilgrims, and set down the mystical Revelations that made her famous throughout Christendom. Not long before her death she completed a pilgrimage to the Holy Land.

She died at Rome on the twenty-third of July 1373. Her body was carried back to Sweden and enshrined at the abbey of Vadstena, the mother house of the Bridgettine order she had founded; she was canonized in 1391.

events.title: The death of Thomas à Kempis
events.shortBlurb: The canon of the Devotio Moderna died at Mount St. Agnes, long held to be author of the Imitation of Christ…
body: Thomas Haemerken of Kempen, known as Thomas à Kempis, was a canon regular formed in the Devotio Moderna, the movement of interior renewal that flourished in the Low Countries. He passed most of his long life in the monastery of Mount St. Agnes near Zwolle, copying manuscripts, writing, and directing souls in the ways of humility and prayer.
He died there on the twenty-fifth of July 1471. He is by long tradition regarded as the author of The Imitation of Christ, after the Scriptures among the most widely read of all Christian books.

events.title: The fall of Robespierre and the end of the Terror
events.shortBlurb: The execution of Robespierre brought the Reign of Terror to a close and eased the persecution of the Church…
body: Maximilien Robespierre, the dominant figure of the Committee of Public Safety, had presided over the Reign of Terror in which thousands were sent to the guillotine, among them many priests, religious, and faithful who would not submit to the revolutionary church. Turned upon by his own colleagues in the Convention, he was arrested and, on the twenty-eighth of July 1794, guillotined.

His death broke the machinery of the Terror and brought its executions to an end. For the Church in France, savagely persecuted in those years, it opened the way to a gradual respite from the worst of the bloodshed.

events.title: St. Olaf falls at Stiklestad
events.shortBlurb: The king who worked to Christianize Norway was killed in battle and became the nation's patron…
body: Olaf Haraldsson, king of Norway, labored to unite his realm and to root the Christian faith firmly in the land, sometimes by forceful means that stirred the opposition of the great chieftains. Driven into exile, he returned to reclaim his kingdom and met his enemies in battle at Stiklestad.

There, on the twenty-ninth of July 1030, he was killed. Miracles were soon reported at his grave, and he was venerated as a martyr and saint; honored as Rex Perpetuus Norvegiae, the eternal king of Norway, he became the patron of the nation whose conversion he had advanced.

events.title: The First Defenestration of Prague
events.shortBlurb: Hussite crowds threw the town councillors from the windows of the New Town Hall, igniting the Hussite Wars…
body: Four years after the burning of Jan Hus, his followers in Bohemia were in open agitation against the authorities. On the thirtieth of July 1419 a procession of Hussites led by the radical preacher Jan Želivský marched to the New Town Hall of Prague, and in the tumult that followed the Catholic town councillors were seized and hurled from the windows to the crowd below, who killed them.
The outrage set off the Hussite Wars, a long and destructive conflict between the Hussite factions and the Catholic crown and Church that would trouble central Europe for years to come.

events.title: The death of St. Ignatius of Loyola
events.shortBlurb: The founder of the Society of Jesus died at Rome as his young order spread across the world…
body: St. Ignatius of Loyola governed the Society of Jesus from Rome as its first general, sending his companions across Europe and to the missions of Asia, Africa, and the New World, and founding colleges that made the order a great force in education. He guided the swiftly growing Society by letters and by the Constitutions he composed.

He died quietly at Rome on the thirty-first of July 1556; by then the order he had begun with a handful of companions numbered about a thousand members. He was beatified in 1609 and canonized in 1622.

events.title: The Pardon of Assisi
events.shortBlurb: The great indulgence tradition holds St. Francis obtained for pilgrims to the little chapel of the Portiuncula…
body: The Portiuncula, or Little Portion, was the small, ruined chapel of St. Mary of the Angels near Assisi that St. Francis restored with his own hands and made the cradle of the Franciscan Order. It was here that he understood his call to poverty and gathered his first brothers.

A cherished Franciscan tradition, dated to about 1216, tells that Francis begged and obtained from Pope Honorius III a plenary indulgence, the Pardon of Assisi, for all who, truly repentant and having confessed, should visit the chapel. The pious observance spread widely and is kept each year on 2 August, extended in time to Franciscan and parish churches.

events.title: The martyrdom of Pope St. Sixtus II
events.shortBlurb: A pope was cut down with his deacons at the altar in the Roman catacombs under the persecution of Valerian…
body: In 258 the Emperor Valerian issued a savage edict commanding that Christian bishops, priests, and deacons be put to death at once. On 6 August of that year Pope Sixtus II was seized while seated to preach and celebrate the liturgy in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way.

He was beheaded together with several of his deacons, and his archdeacon Lawrence would follow him in martyrdom four days later. The death of a pope at the very altar left a deep mark on the Roman Church, which entered the name of Sixtus into the Canon of the Mass among its most honored martyrs.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Paul VI
events.shortBlurb: The pope who brought the Second Vatican Council to its close died on the feast of the Transfiguration…
body: Giovanni Battista Montini, born near Brescia in 1897, was elected pope in 1963 and took the name Paul VI. To him fell the task of guiding the Second Vatican Council through its final sessions and of carrying out its reforms, including the revision of the Roman Missal, while striving to hold the Church together amid great upheaval.

He was the first pope in modern times to travel widely, journeying to the Holy Land and to five continents, and he taught the Church in landmark documents on human life, development, and evangelization. He died at the papal residence of Castel Gandolfo on the evening of 6 August 1978, the feast of the Transfiguration, and was himself canonized in 2018.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Paul VI (vatican.va)

events.title: The Battle of Lechfeld
events.shortBlurb: The defeat of the raiding Magyars by Otto the Great turned Hungary toward settlement and the Christian faith…
body: For decades the mounted Magyars had ravaged the lands of Western Christendom, striking as far as France and Italy and terrorizing the frontier of Germany. In August 955 they laid siege to Augsburg, whose bishop St. Ulrich rallied the townsfolk to hold the walls until help could come.

On 10 August King Otto I, later crowned emperor, met and crushed the Magyar host on the Lechfeld near Augsburg. The victory ended the great raids and helped turn the Magyars from plunder to settlement in the Danube basin, opening the way, within two generations, to their conversion under St. Stephen and the birth of Christian Hungary.

events.title: The founding of the Society of Jesus
events.shortBlurb: On the feast of the Assumption, Ignatius of Loyola and his companions bound themselves by vow at Montmartre…
body: St. Ignatius of Loyola, a former soldier converted during a long recovery from a battle wound, had gathered around him at the University of Paris a small band of devoted companions, among them St. Francis Xavier and Bl. Peter Faber. Together they resolved to give their lives wholly to the service of God.

On 15 August 1534, the feast of the Assumption, the little group climbed to a chapel at Montmartre in Paris and bound themselves by vows of poverty and chastity and a promise to labor for souls, whether in the Holy Land or wherever the pope should send them. From this beginning grew the Society of Jesus, formally approved by Pope Paul III in 1540, which would become a great force in education, missions, and the renewal of the Church.

events.title: The sack of Rome by Alaric
events.shortBlurb: The Visigoths breached the walls of the eternal city, shaking the ancient world and moving Augustine to write…
body: On 24 August 410 the Visigoths under their king Alaric entered Rome and plundered it for three days. Though the city was no longer the seat of empire, its fall to a foreign enemy for the first time in some eight hundred years sent a tremor of dismay through the whole Roman world; from Bethlehem St. Jerome wrote that the light of the world had been put out.

Alaric, an Arian Christian, spared those who took refuge in the great basilicas of the apostles, and Rome was not destroyed. Pagans blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the old gods, and to answer them St. Augustine began his vast work The City of God, contrasting the passing city of man with the eternal city of God.

events.title: The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre
events.shortBlurb: A wave of killing of French Protestants that began in Paris on the feast of St. Bartholomew stands as one of the tragedies of the Wars of Religion…
body: In the summer of 1572 Paris was crowded for the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre to the Catholic princess Margaret of Valois, a match meant to reconcile a France torn by religious war. Instead, in the tense days that followed, the crown moved against the leaders of the Huguenot party gathered in the city.

Beginning in the night before the feast of St. Bartholomew, 24 August, the killing of Huguenot nobles spread into a general massacre of Protestants in Paris and then in provincial cities over the following weeks, leaving many thousands dead. The bloodshed deepened and prolonged the French Wars of Religion, and later ages have remembered it soberly as a grievous crime committed in the tangled strife of faith and politics.

events.title: The death of St. Louis IX on crusade
events.shortBlurb: The holy king of France died of disease in the crusader camp before the walls of Tunis…
body: Having already been captured and ransomed on an earlier crusade to Egypt, King Louis IX of France took the cross a second time and in 1270 led his army to North Africa, landing near the city of Tunis. There the crusaders were struck by an epidemic that swept through the camp in the summer heat.

Louis himself fell ill and died on 25 August 1270, his last thoughts, according to those present, turned to Jerusalem and to the spread of the faith. His bones were carried back to France and laid to rest at Saint-Denis, and the king who had ruled with such justice was canonized within a generation.

events.title: The Battle of Manzikert
events.shortBlurb: The Byzantine defeat that opened Asia Minor to the Turks and set the stage for the Crusades…
body: On 26 August 1071, near Manzikert in Armenia, the army of the Byzantine emperor Romanus IV Diogenes was defeated by the Seljuk Turks under Alp Arslan, and the emperor himself was taken prisoner. The disaster shattered the eastern defenses of the Christian empire.

In the years that followed the Turks pressed deep into Asia Minor, the ancient heartland of Eastern Christianity, overrunning its cities and bishoprics. The peril to the Christian East, and the appeals of the Byzantine emperors to the West, would help move Pope Urban II a generation later to summon the First Crusade.

events.title: The death of Pope Sixtus V
events.shortBlurb: The vigorous reforming pope who rebuilt Rome and reorganized the Curia died after a brief but momentous reign…
body: Felice Peretti, a Franciscan of humble birth, was elected pope in 1585 and took the name Sixtus V. In only five years he transformed the government of the Church and the face of its capital, fixing the number of cardinals and establishing the permanent congregations through which the Curia would be administered for centuries.

He restored order to the Papal States by stern justice against banditry, completed the great dome of St. Peter's, raised the Vatican obelisk, and brought fresh water to Rome through a new aqueduct. He also promoted a corrected edition of the Latin Vulgate; when he died on 27 August 1590 he left behind a Rome and a papal administration deeply reshaped by his energy.

events.title: The death of St. Augustine and the siege of Hippo
events.shortBlurb: The great bishop and Doctor died as the Vandals pressed their siege against his African city…
body: By 430 the Vandals under Genseric had crossed from Spain into Roman Africa, ravaging the provinces and laying siege to the coastal city of Hippo, where Augustine had been bishop for more than thirty years. Refugees and fellow bishops crowded into the city, and Augustine counseled his clergy to remain with their people in the danger.

In the third month of the siege, on 28 August 430, Augustine died, having spent his last days in prayer and penance with the psalms posted on the wall before him. His passing marked the end of an age for the Church of Roman Africa, but his writings, carried westward, would shape Christian thought for a thousand years and more.

events.title: The Battle of Mohács
events.shortBlurb: The Ottoman victory that broke the kingdom of Hungary and opened Central Europe to Turkish advance…
body: On 29 August 1526, on the plain of Mohács by the Danube, the army of the young King Louis II of Hungary was overwhelmed by the far larger forces of the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. The king himself perished in flight, and with him fell much of the Hungarian nobility and many bishops.

The catastrophe shattered the medieval kingdom of Hungary, long a bulwark of Christendom against the Turks, and led to its partition and to generations of Ottoman occupation of its central lands. The Turkish advance would press on toward Vienna, keeping Central Europe under the shadow of war for more than a century.

events.title: The September Massacres of Paris
events.shortBlurb: Revolutionary mobs stormed the Paris prisons and slaughtered priests and religious who had refused the oath against the Church…
body: In the first days of September 1792, as the French Revolution turned to terror and foreign armies advanced on Paris, crowds broke into the city's crowded prisons and killed those held within. Among the first to die, on 2 September, were the priests and religious detained at the former Carmelite convent in the Rue de Vaugirard, cut down for refusing to swear the Civil Constitution of the Clergy that would have separated them from Rome.

The killings spread through the prisons over several days and claimed well over a thousand lives, of whom hundreds were clergy. One hundred and ninety-one of these churchmen — bishops, priests, and religious — were later recognized as martyrs and beatified by Pope Pius XI in 1926. Their deaths mark one of the bloodiest episodes of the Revolution's assault on the Church in France.

events.title: St. Gregory the Great is consecrated Pope
events.shortBlurb: The reluctant monk was consecrated Bishop of Rome and began a pontificate that would reshape the medieval Church…
body: On 3 September 590 Gregory, a monk drawn unwillingly from his monastery, was consecrated Bishop of Rome amid plague, famine, and the ruin left by the Lombard wars. He had tried to escape the office, but the clergy and people of the city insisted, and he took up a burden he compared to a storm-tossed ship.

His fourteen-year pontificate fed the poor of Rome from the Church's estates, negotiated with the invading Lombards, reformed the liturgy and its chant, and sent Augustine and his monks to convert the English. Styling himself "servant of the servants of God," a title the popes bear still, Gregory did much to define the papacy for the ages that followed.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "Pope St. Gregory I (the Great)"

events.title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.shortBlurb: The last emperor in the West was deposed, and the Church became the enduring institution of a collapsing world…
body: On 4 September 476, the barbarian commander Odoacer deposed the boy-emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna, and no emperor reigned again in the West. Historians long marked the date as the end of the Western Roman Empire, though the change was less a single fall than the last step of a long decline.

As Roman civil authority dissolved, the Catholic Church remained the one institution spanning the former empire, and its bishops — above all the Bishop of Rome — increasingly took up the ordering of society, the care of cities, and the preservation of learning. St. Augustine, who had died a generation before as the Vandals besieged his city, had already taught the Church to look beyond the earthly city to the City of God.

events.title: The lifting of the Great Siege of Malta
events.shortBlurb: The Knights of St. John broke the Ottoman siege of Malta, and Christendom credited the deliverance to Our Lady on the feast of her Nativity…
body: Through the summer of 1565 a great Ottoman fleet and army besieged the small island of Malta, held by the Knights of St. John under their aged Grand Master, Jean Parisot de Valette. Against enormous odds the knights, soldiers, and Maltese people held the forts through months of bombardment and assault at appalling cost.

In early September a relief force from Sicily landed, and the exhausted Ottoman army abandoned the siege, withdrawing about the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 8 September. The victory, celebrated across Europe as a deliverance of Christendom, was widely attributed to the intercession of Our Lady, and the day was long kept in Malta with thanksgiving.

events.title: The relief of Vienna
events.shortBlurb: A Christian army under John III Sobieski broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna, and the pope extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary in thanksgiving…
body: By September 1683 the Ottoman army had besieged Vienna for two months, and the fall of the city would have opened central Europe to the Turks. On 12 September a relief army led by King John III Sobieski of Poland, together with imperial and German forces gathered by the appeals of Pope Innocent XI, descended from the Kahlenberg heights and shattered the besiegers in a great battle.

The deliverance was received as a victory of Christendom, and the Capuchin friar Marco d'Aviano, who had preached to the troops, was among those who gave thanks. In gratitude Pope Innocent XI extended the feast of the Most Holy Name of Mary, kept on the anniversary of the battle, to the whole Church.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "The Holy Name of Mary"

events.title: The death of St. John Chrysostom in exile
events.shortBlurb: The great preacher and archbishop of Constantinople died on the road of a second banishment, blessing God to the end…
body: John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople, had been driven from his see by the hostility of the imperial court and of bishops whose worldliness he rebuked. Condemned to exile in a remote corner of the empire, he was marched on foot in harsh weather toward the far shore of the Black Sea.

Worn out by the journey, he died at Comana in Pontus on 14 September 407, his last words reported as "Glory to God for all things." Because 14 September later held the feast of the Holy Cross, the West keeps his memorial on the thirteenth. Decades after his death his relics were returned in honour to Constantinople, and he is venerated as a Doctor of the Church.

events.title: The dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
events.shortBlurb: Constantine's great basilica over Calvary and the tomb of Christ was dedicated at Jerusalem, giving rise to the feast of the Holy Cross…
body: In 335 the basilica raised by the Emperor Constantine over the site of Calvary and the Holy Sepulchre was solemnly dedicated at Jerusalem. Near this place, tradition held, St. Helena, the emperor's mother, had discovered the True Cross of Christ, and a relic of it was thereafter venerated in the city.

From the annual commemoration of this dedication and the showing of the Cross grew the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. Its observance was deepened in 629, when the Emperor Heraclius restored to Jerusalem the relic of the Cross that the Persians had carried away — an event long celebrated on this day together with the dedication.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Cyprian of Carthage
events.shortBlurb: The bishop and great writer of the African Church was beheaded before his people in the persecution of Valerian…
body: St. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and one of the foremost Latin writers of the early Church, had guided his flock through persecution and plague and through the bitter controversy over the readmission of those who had lapsed. When the persecution of the Emperor Valerian struck the leaders of the Church, Cyprian was arrested and sentenced.

On 14 September 258 he was led out and beheaded near Carthage in the presence of a great crowd of the faithful, having first blessed God and provided for the executioner's fee. His memorial is kept on 16 September together with Pope Cornelius, whom he had defended a few years before and who had himself died for the faith in exile.

events.title: The stigmata of St. Francis of Assisi
events.shortBlurb: On the mountain of La Verna, St. Francis received in his own body the wounds of the crucified Christ…
body: In September 1224, while keeping a fast in honour of St. Michael on the lonely heights of Mount La Verna in the Apennines, Francis of Assisi was absorbed in prayer over the Passion of Christ. According to his early companions, he beheld a vision of a seraph bearing the figure of the Crucified, and when it passed there appeared in his hands, feet, and side the marks of the wounds of Christ.

Francis strove to hide these stigmata for the two years that remained to him before his death in 1226. The event, the first such recorded in the Church, was celebrated as a singular seal upon his likeness to the crucified Lord, and the Franciscan order keeps its memorial on 17 September.

events.title: The apparition of Our Lady of La Salette
events.shortBlurb: On a mountainside in the French Alps a weeping Lady appeared to two shepherd children with a call to penance and prayer…
body: On 19 September 1846, two young shepherds, Mélanie Calvat and Maximin Giraud, saw upon a mountain near the village of La Salette in the French Alps a brilliant figure of a weeping woman seated on a stone. She spoke to them of the neglect of Sunday and of the name of God, calling her people to conversion, prayer, and penance, and entrusting each child with a secret.

After careful examination the apparition was approved for the faithful's devotion by the bishop of Grenoble in 1851, and a great basilica and shrine rose on the mountain. Our Lady of La Salette, the reconciler of sinners, has been honoured ever since as a summons to repentance.

events.title: The capture of Rome and the end of the Papal States
events.shortBlurb: Italian troops breached the walls at the Porta Pia, ending eleven centuries of papal temporal rule over Rome…
body: On 20 September 1870, after the withdrawal of the French garrison that had protected the city, the army of the Kingdom of Italy bombarded and breached the walls of Rome at the Porta Pia. Pope Pius IX, unwilling to see blood shed in a hopeless defence, ordered his small force to lay down its arms after a brief resistance.

With the fall of the city the Papal States, which had existed in some form for more than a thousand years, came to an end, and Rome became the capital of united Italy. Pius IX withdrew within the Vatican and declared himself a "prisoner," beginning the long estrangement between the Holy See and the Italian state that would not be settled until the Lateran agreements of 1929.

events.title: The founding of the Order of Our Lady of Ransom
events.shortBlurb: St. Peter Nolasco founded an order vowed to ransom Christian captives from the Moors, honoured under the title of Our Lady of Ransom…
body: In the early thirteenth century, with much of Spain under Moorish rule and many Christians held captive, Peter Nolasco of Barcelona was moved to devote himself to their ransom. According to the order's tradition the Blessed Virgin Mary made known her desire for such a work, and in 1218, with the counsel of St. Raymond of Peñafort and the support of King James I of Aragon, the Order of Our Lady of Mercy — the Mercedarians — was founded.

Its members took a special fourth vow to give even themselves, if need be, as hostages for the deliverance of captives in danger of losing their faith. The order spread through Spain and the New World, and the commemoration of Our Lady of Ransom on 24 September grew from its devotion.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "The Order of Our Lady of Mercy"

events.title: The papal approval of the Society of Jesus
events.shortBlurb: Pope Paul III confirmed the new order gathered by Ignatius of Loyola, launching the Jesuits into the service of the Church…
body: On 27 September 1540 Pope Paul III issued the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae, giving canonical approval to the Society of Jesus, the company of priests gathered around Ignatius of Loyola and his first companions, who had bound themselves by vows and offered their service to the pope. Ignatius was chosen its first superior general the following year.

Marked by disciplined obedience, rigorous formation, and a special vow to the Holy Father, the Society threw itself into preaching, education, and missions. Within a generation its members — Francis Xavier in the East, others across Europe and the New World — had made it one of the chief instruments of the Catholic reform.

events.title: St. Jerome and the Latin Vulgate
events.shortBlurb: The scholar who gave the Latin Church its Bible died at Bethlehem, leaving a translation that would shape Western Christianity for a thousand years…
body: Commissioned by Pope Damasus to set in order the Latin texts of Scripture then in circulation, Jerome devoted the labour of decades — much of it in a cell at Bethlehem — to translating and revising the Bible, going back for the Old Testament to the original Hebrew rather than relying only on the Greek. The version that resulted, later called the Vulgate, became the common Bible of the Western Church.

Jerome died at Bethlehem about the year 420. His translation would be read, copied, and expounded throughout the Middle Ages, and at the Council of Trent it was declared the Church's authentic Latin text. His life's insistence — that "ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ" — has been echoed by the Church ever since.

events.title: The death of St. Francis of Assisi
events.shortBlurb: The Poverello died at the Portiuncula near Assisi; his passing is kept by the Franciscans as the Transitus…
body: On the evening of 3 October 1226 Francis of Assisi died at the little chapel of the Portiuncula outside the walls of his city, having asked to be laid naked upon the bare ground so as to meet death in the poverty he had loved all his life. He was about forty-five years old, worn out by austerity, illness, and the wounds of the stigmata he had borne since Mount La Verna.

In his last days he added to his Canticle of the Creatures a verse in praise of “Sister Bodily Death,” and asked that the Passion account of St. John be read to him. His feast is kept the following day, 4 October. Less than two years after his death he was canonized by Pope Gregory IX, and the great basilica at Assisi rose over his tomb.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 October

events.title: The victory of Lepanto
events.shortBlurb: A Christian fleet of the Holy League turned back the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Corinth; the day gave rise to the feast of the Rosary…
body: On 7 October 1571 the fleet of the Holy League, assembled by Pope St. Pius V from Spain, Venice, the Papal States, and other Catholic powers under the command of Don John of Austria, met the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Lepanto off the coast of Greece. In one of the largest naval battles of the age, fought with hundreds of galleys and tens of thousands of men, the Christian fleet won a decisive victory and broke the momentum of Turkish expansion in the Mediterranean.

Pope Pius V had called on the faithful of Europe to pray the Rosary for the outcome, and he attributed the deliverance to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary. In thanksgiving he instituted an annual commemoration, later established as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary, kept on the anniversary of the battle.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Holy Rosary”

events.title: The opening of the Second Vatican Council
events.shortBlurb: Pope John XXIII opened the twenty-first ecumenical council before a great gathering of the world's bishops…
body: On 11 October 1962 Pope John XXIII solemnly opened the Second Vatican Council in the basilica of St. Peter, with more than two thousand bishops from around the world in attendance, the largest such gathering in the Church's history. In his opening address, Gaudet Mater Ecclesia, the pope set out his hope that the Council would present the unchanging faith in a way suited to the needs of the age.

Over four sessions, continuing under Pope Paul VI until 1965, the Council produced sixteen documents on the liturgy, the Church, revelation, and the Church's relation to the modern world. Its decisions, including the reform of the liturgy and a renewed emphasis on the universal call to holiness, profoundly shaped Catholic life in the decades that followed. The 11th of October was later chosen as the memorial of St. John XXIII, who had convoked it.

sources.text: Vatican, Documents of the Second Vatican Council (vatican.va)

events.title: The landfall in the New World
events.shortBlurb: Columbus reached an island of the Americas, opening the way for the Christian evangelization of a continent…
body: In the early hours of 12 October 1492 the expedition of Christopher Columbus, sailing under the patronage of the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, sighted land in the islands of the Caribbean after weeks at sea. Columbus named the first island San Salvador, “Holy Saviour,” and planted a cross, understanding his voyage in part as a mission to carry the faith to unknown peoples.

Whatever the mixed and often tragic consequences of the encounter that followed, it opened the way for the coming of Franciscan, Dominican, Jesuit, and other missionaries to the Americas. Within a generation friars were preaching, baptizing, and, like the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos and later Bartolomé de las Casas, raising their voices in defense of the native peoples against the cruelty of the conquerors.

events.title: The Miracle of the Sun at Fatima
events.shortBlurb: A great crowd at Fatima reported seeing the sun spin and plunge toward the earth after the apparitions to three shepherd children…
body: On 13 October 1917 a large crowd, numbering in the tens of thousands, gathered in a field at the Cova da Iria near Fatima in Portugal, where three shepherd children, Lúcia, Francisco, and Jacinta, had reported a series of apparitions of the Blessed Virgin Mary since the previous May. The children had foretold that on this day a sign would be given so that all might believe.

According to numerous witnesses, including some initially hostile to the claims, the rain-soaked crowd saw the clouds part and the sun appear to spin, throw off colors, and plunge toward the earth before returning to its place, after which their drenched clothing was found dry. The apparitions of Our Lady of Fatima, with their call to prayer, penance, and the Rosary, were later approved for devotion by the local bishop, and the events became one of the most influential of modern Marian devotions.

sources.text: Vatican, The Message of Fatima (Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 2000; vatican.va)

events.title: The Gregorian calendar begins
events.shortBlurb: By decree of Pope Gregory XIII the calendar leapt from 4 October straight to 15 October to correct the drift of the seasons…
body: The Julian calendar in use since Roman times had gained too many days over the centuries, so that the date of the spring equinox, on which the calculation of Easter depended, had drifted well away from its true place. In his bull Inter gravissimas of 1582, Pope Gregory XIII, acting on the work of astronomers including Christopher Clavius and Aloysius Lilius, ordered a reform.

To restore the equinox to its proper date, ten days were dropped from the calendar: the day after Thursday, 4 October 1582 became Friday, 15 October. A revised rule for leap years was adopted to keep the calendar in step with the sun over the long term. Catholic countries adopted the new reckoning at once, while many Protestant and Orthodox lands accepted it only over the following centuries. It remains the civil calendar of most of the world today.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “The Reform of the Calendar”

events.title: The election of Pope John Paul II
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals chose Karol Wojtyła of Kraków, the first non-Italian pope in more than four centuries…
body: On 16 October 1978, in a conclave held after the sudden death of Pope John Paul I, the College of Cardinals elected Karol Wojtyła, the fifty-eight-year-old Archbishop of Kraków in Poland. He was the first pope from Poland and the first non-Italian to hold the office since the sixteenth century, and he took the name John Paul II in continuity with his short-lived predecessor.

His nearly twenty-seven-year pontificate became one of the longest and most consequential in history. He traveled the world, addressed the young, defended the dignity of the human person, and played a notable part in the peaceful collapse of communism in eastern Europe. Presenting himself to the crowd, he urged the world in words that became a keynote of his ministry: “Be not afraid.”

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope John Paul II (vatican.va)

events.title: The Battle of the Milvian Bridge
events.shortBlurb: Constantine conquered under the sign of the Cross, opening the way to the toleration of Christianity…
body: On 28 October 312 the armies of Constantine and his rival Maxentius met at the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber, north of Rome. According to the accounts of the Christian writers Lactantius and Eusebius, Constantine had been moved before the battle by a heavenly sign, a cross of light with the words “In this sign you will conquer,” and ordered the Christian monogram, the Chi-Rho, placed on the shields of his soldiers.

Constantine won a complete victory; Maxentius drowned in the river as his forces fled. The battle made Constantine master of the West, and within months, by the Edict of Milan in 313, he granted the Christians of the empire freedom to practice their faith. The long age of persecution came to an end, and the Church emerged from the catacombs into public life.

events.title: The election of Pope John XXIII
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals chose the aged Angelo Roncalli, who would surprise the world by summoning a council…
body: On 28 October 1958, after the death of Pope Pius XII, the College of Cardinals elected Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli, the Patriarch of Venice, who took the name John XXIII. Nearly seventy-seven years old and widely expected to be a brief, transitional pope, he was chosen in part for his warmth and pastoral experience.

Within three months of his election he astonished the Church by announcing his intention to convoke an ecumenical council. That council, the Second Vatican Council, would open in 1962 and shape the life of the Catholic Church for generations. Beloved as “Good Pope John,” he was canonized in 2014.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope John XXIII (vatican.va)

events.title: Luther posts the Ninety-Five Theses
events.shortBlurb: At Wittenberg an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther set out ninety-five theses against the preaching of indulgences — the spark, by long tradition, of the Protestant Reformation…
body: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, published ninety-five theses disputing the preaching of indulgences. What began as an academic protest widened rapidly into a break with the Church that divided Western Christendom.
In answer the Church undertook the reform and definition of doctrine at the Council of Trent (1545–1563), the great work of the Catholic Reformation.

events.title: The Sistine Chapel ceiling unveiled
events.shortBlurb: On All Saints' Day, Michelangelo's newly completed ceiling of the Sistine Chapel was shown for the first time…
body: On All Saints' Day in 1512, the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican, painted by Michelangelo Buonarroti over some four years, was uncovered and seen for the first time as Pope Julius II celebrated Mass beneath it.

Across the vast vault Michelangelo had set the story of creation and the fall, the great figures of prophets and sibyls, and the ancestors of Christ, in one of the supreme achievements of Christian art. The chapel, which serves for the most solemn papal ceremonies and for the conclaves that elect the pope, has been adorned by it ever since.

events.title: The Lisbon earthquake
events.shortBlurb: A catastrophic earthquake struck Lisbon on All Saints' Day as the churches were full for Mass…
body: On the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, a tremendous earthquake struck Lisbon while the churches of the Portuguese capital were crowded for the feast. The shocks, followed by a great sea wave and by fires that raged for days, destroyed much of the city and killed tens of thousands.

The disaster, falling on a holy day and levelling churches with the rest, shook the confidence of eighteenth-century Europe and provoked long debate among philosophers and theologians on the problem of suffering and divine providence. It remains one of the most consequential natural catastrophes in European history.

events.title: The dogma of the Assumption defined
events.shortBlurb: Pope Pius XII solemnly defined that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heaven…
body: On 1 November 1950, in the Apostolic Constitution Munificentissimus Deus, Pope Pius XII solemnly defined as a dogma of the Catholic faith that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever-Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory.

The definition gathered up an ancient belief long celebrated in the liturgy of both East and West and confirmed by the faith of the whole Church. It remains the most recent exercise of the extraordinary papal magisterium in defining a dogma, proclaimed before an immense throng in St. Peter's Square during the Holy Year.

sources.text: Apostolic Constitution Munificentissimus Deus, Pope Pius XII (vatican.va)

events.title: St. Odilo institutes the commemoration of all the departed
events.shortBlurb: The abbot of Cluny fixed a yearly day of prayer for all the faithful dead, the origin of All Souls' Day…
body: Near the end of the tenth century, St. Odilo, the great abbot of Cluny, decreed that all the monasteries under his rule should keep, on the day after the feast of All Saints, a solemn commemoration of all the faithful departed, with prayers, Masses, and alms offered for their souls.

From the Cluniac houses the observance spread rapidly through the Western Church until it became the universal All Souls' Day. It gave lasting liturgical form to the ancient Christian practice of praying for the dead and to the doctrine of purgatory and the communion of saints.

events.title: The Act of Supremacy
events.shortBlurb: The English Parliament declared King Henry VIII the Supreme Head of the Church of England, severing it from Rome…
body: In November 1534 the English Parliament, reassembling for the session in which it completed the work of the royal Reformation, passed the Act of Supremacy, which declared King Henry VIII to be the Supreme Head on earth of the Church of England and repudiated the authority of the Pope in the realm.

The breach followed the king's failed attempt to obtain from Rome the annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. The refusal to swear to the new supremacy would cost the lives of St. John Fisher, St. Thomas More, and many others, and opened three centuries of penal law against Catholics in England.

events.title: The Gunpowder Plot discovered
events.shortBlurb: A conspiracy by a group of English Catholics to blow up Parliament was uncovered on the eve of its opening…
body: In the early hours of 5 November 1605, a plot to destroy the King and Parliament of England was discovered when Guy Fawkes was found guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath the House of Lords. The conspirators, a small band of desperate Catholic gentlemen led by Robert Catesby, had hoped by the explosion to end the persecution of their faith.

The plot failed utterly, and its discovery brought disaster upon English Catholics, who as a body had neither part in nor knowledge of it. New and harsher penal laws followed, and the memory of the conspiracy long inflamed suspicion of the old religion in England.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Leo the Great
events.shortBlurb: One of the greatest of the early popes died at Rome, leaving the faith of Chalcedon secured…
body: On 10 November 461 Pope St. Leo I, called the Great, died at Rome after a pontificate of more than twenty years. He had governed the Church through the collapse of Roman power in the West and had raised the See of Peter to a new height of moral authority.

His dogmatic letter, the Tome of Leo, had guided the Council of Chalcedon in 451 to define the two natures in the one person of Christ; in 452 he had gone out to meet Attila the Hun and turned him back from Rome. A great preacher and pastor, he was later numbered among the Doctors of the Church.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Leo I (the Great)”

events.title: The Fourth Lateran Council opens
events.shortBlurb: The greatest council of the medieval West opened in Rome under Pope Innocent III…
body: On 11 November 1215 Pope Innocent III opened the Fourth Lateran Council in Rome, gathering hundreds of bishops and abbots and the representatives of Christian princes in what was the most important council of the medieval Church.

Its decrees shaped Catholic life for centuries: it employed the term transubstantiation in teaching on the Eucharist, required the faithful to confess and receive Communion at least once a year at Easter, ordered reform of the clergy, and set in motion much of the pastoral renewal of the thirteenth century.

events.title: The martyrs of the Central American University
events.shortBlurb: Six Jesuit priests and two women were murdered in San Salvador during the country's civil war…
body: In the early hours of 16 November 1989, at the Central American University in San Salvador, soldiers killed six Jesuit priests — among them the rector, Ignacio Ellacuría — together with their housekeeper and her young daughter. The Jesuits had been outspoken voices for justice and for a negotiated end to El Salvador's civil war.

The killings drew the attention of the world to the sufferings of the Salvadoran people and to the cost of the Church's defence of the poor. The victims are remembered among the many who gave their lives for faith and justice in the turmoil of Central America in those years.

sources.text: Vatican / Holy See communications on the martyrs of El Salvador (vatican.va)

events.title: The bull Unam Sanctam
events.shortBlurb: Pope Boniface VIII issued his celebrated declaration on the unity of the Church and the authority of the Pope…
body: On 18 November 1302, amid a bitter conflict with King Philip the Fair of France, Pope Boniface VIII issued the bull Unam Sanctam, one of the strongest of all papal statements on the authority of the Roman See.

The bull affirmed that there is one holy Catholic and apostolic Church outside which there is no salvation, and concluded by declaring it necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff. It became a classic text in later debates over the relation of spiritual and temporal power.

events.title: The new St. Peter's Basilica consecrated
events.shortBlurb: Pope Urban VIII consecrated the rebuilt Basilica of St. Peter in Rome, more than a century in the making…
body: On 18 November 1626 Pope Urban VIII solemnly consecrated the new Basilica of St. Peter in the Vatican, the greatest church of Western Christendom, raised over the tomb of the Apostle in place of the ancient basilica of Constantine.

The rebuilding had occupied more than a hundred and twenty years and the genius of a succession of architects, among them Bramante, Michelangelo, who designed its great dome, and Maderno. The date was chosen to fall on the anniversary of the dedication of the old basilica, kept in the Roman calendar as the feast of the dedication of the churches of Sts. Peter and Paul.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “The Basilica of St. Peter”

events.title: Lumen Gentium promulgated
events.shortBlurb: The Second Vatican Council promulgated its Dogmatic Constitution on the Church…
body: On 21 November 1964, at the close of its third session, the Second Vatican Council promulgated Lumen Gentium, the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, one of the central documents of the Council. It presented the Church as the People of God and the mystical Body of Christ, taught the universal call to holiness, and set forth the doctrine of the college of bishops.

On the same day the Council promulgated its Decree on Ecumenism and its Decree on the Eastern Catholic Churches, and Pope Paul VI proclaimed the Blessed Virgin Mary Mother of the Church. Together these acts marked one of the great days of the Council's work of renewal.

sources.text: Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium (vatican.va)

events.title: The martyrdom of Blessed Miguel Pro
events.shortBlurb: A young Mexican Jesuit was shot by a firing squad, crying out his love for Christ the King…
body: On 23 November 1927, during the fierce anti-Catholic persecution in Mexico, the Jesuit priest Miguel Agustín Pro was executed by firing squad on a false charge, without trial. In defiance of the ban on public worship he had ministered in secret to the faithful of Mexico City, bringing the sacraments in disguise.

Refusing a blindfold, he stretched out his arms in the form of a cross and, as the soldiers took aim, cried out Viva Cristo Rey — Long live Christ the King. Photographs of his death, meant to intimidate, instead spread his fame. He was beatified in 1988 and is remembered among the martyrs of the Mexican persecution.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Beatification of Blessed Miguel Agustín Pro (vatican.va)

events.title: Urban II preaches the First Crusade at Clermont
events.shortBlurb: At the Council of Clermont Pope Urban II called Christendom to aid the Eastern churches and free the holy places, and the crowd is said to have answered, “Deus vult” — God wills it…
body: At the close of the Council of Clermont in France, on 27 November 1095, Pope Urban II preached to a great throng, urging the knights of the West to cease their private wars and go to the aid of the Christians of the East and the holy places of Jerusalem.
The response, tradition records, was the cry “Deus vult” — God wills it — and the taking of the cross. So began the First Crusade, which reached Jerusalem in 1099.

events.title: The apparition of the Miraculous Medal
events.shortBlurb: The Blessed Virgin Mary appeared to St. Catherine Labouré in Paris and asked that a medal be struck…
body: On 27 November 1830, in the chapel of the Daughters of Charity on the Rue du Bac in Paris, the young novice Catherine Labouré beheld the Blessed Virgin Mary standing upon a globe, rays of light streaming from her hands. Around the image ran the words, O Mary conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.

Our Lady asked that a medal be struck to this pattern, promising graces to those who wore it with confidence. The medal, first minted in 1832, spread rapidly throughout the world and came to be called the Miraculous Medal for the favours attributed to it. Catherine kept her part hidden until the end of her life.

sources.text: Vatican biography, St. Catherine Labouré and the Miraculous Medal (vatican.va)

events.title: England reconciled to Rome
events.shortBlurb: On the feast of St. Andrew, Cardinal Reginald Pole absolved the realm of England and restored it to communion with the Holy See…
body: On 30 November 1554, the feast of St. Andrew, Cardinal Reginald Pole, papal legate, formally absolved the kingdom of England from the schism of the previous reign and received it back into communion with the Holy See, in the presence of Queen Mary I and the assembled Parliament.

The reconciliation restored, for a few years, the ancient union of England with Rome that Henry VIII had broken. It proved short-lived: with the death of Mary and of Pole in 1558 and the accession of Elizabeth I, the breach with the Holy See was reopened and made lasting.

events.title: Napoleon crowned in the presence of Pius VII
events.shortBlurb: In Notre-Dame de Paris, Napoleon Bonaparte took the imperial crown and set it on his own head while Pope Pius VII looked on…
body: On 2 December 1804, in the cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris, Napoleon Bonaparte was consecrated and crowned Emperor of the French. Pope Pius VII, who had come from Rome for the occasion and had earlier concluded the Concordat of 1801 restoring the Church in France, anointed the emperor; but at the climax Napoleon took the crown and placed it upon his own head, and then crowned his wife Joséphine.

The gesture signified that the new empire would owe its authority to no one, least of all the pope. Relations between Napoleon and Pius VII soon soured: within a few years the emperor annexed the Papal States and held the pope a virtual prisoner in France until 1814.

events.title: The Council of Trent concludes
events.shortBlurb: After eighteen years and twenty-five sessions, the great reforming council of the Catholic Reformation brought its work to a close…
body: On 3–4 December 1563 the Council of Trent held its twenty-fifth and final session and was solemnly closed. Convened in 1545 to answer the Protestant Reformation, the council had defined Catholic teaching on Scripture and Tradition, original sin, justification, the seven sacraments, and the sacrifice of the Mass, and had decreed a thorough reform of the clergy, the founding of seminaries, and the residence of bishops in their dioceses.
Its decrees were confirmed by Pope Pius IV in 1564 and shaped Catholic worship, discipline, and catechesis for four centuries, until the Second Vatican Council.

events.title: St. Thomas Aquinas lays down his pen
events.shortBlurb: After a profound experience at Mass, the greatest of the scholastic theologians ceased to write, saying all he had written seemed like straw…
body: On 6 December 1273, the feast of St. Nicholas, while celebrating Mass at Naples, St. Thomas Aquinas underwent an experience that changed him utterly. From that day he set aside the Summa Theologiae, left unfinished, and wrote no more.

When his companion Reginald of Piperno urged him to continue, Thomas answered that he could write no more, for all that he had written seemed to him like straw compared with what he had seen. He died a few months later, in March 1274, on his way to the Second Council of Lyons.

events.title: Rome and Constantinople lift the anathemas of 1054
events.shortBlurb: On the eve of the Second Vatican Council's close, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras together erased the mutual excommunications that had divided East and West for nine centuries…
body: On 7 December 1965 a common declaration was read simultaneously in Rome, at the Second Vatican Council, and in Constantinople, by which Pope Paul VI and the Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I lifted and committed to oblivion the sentences of mutual excommunication that had been exchanged between their sees in the year 1054.

The act did not by itself restore full communion between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches, but it removed a long-standing sign of the East–West schism and opened a new era of dialogue between the two ancient traditions.

sources.text: Vatican, Common Declaration of Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I (1965) (vatican.va)

events.title: Pius IX defines the Immaculate Conception
events.shortBlurb: In the bull Ineffabilis Deus, Pope Pius IX solemnly defined that the Blessed Virgin Mary was preserved free from original sin from the first moment of her conception…
body: On 8 December 1854, before a great assembly of bishops in St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Pius IX promulgated the Apostolic Constitution Ineffabilis Deus and defined that the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instant of her conception, was preserved immune from all stain of original sin by a singular grace of God and in view of the merits of Jesus Christ.
Four years later, at Lourdes, the apparition who named herself the Immaculate Conception was widely received as heaven's own confirmation of the definition.

events.title: The close of the Second Vatican Council
events.shortBlurb: In St. Peter's Square, Pope Paul VI solemnly brought to an end the twenty-first ecumenical council, the largest in the Church's history…
body: On 8 December 1965, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, Pope Paul VI closed the Second Vatican Council, which had opened under Pope St. John XXIII in 1962. Over four sessions some two and a half thousand bishops from across the world had produced sixteen documents on the Church, divine revelation, the sacred liturgy, the Church in the modern world, ecumenism, and religious liberty.

On the final day the council's messages to humanity were proclaimed, and the assembled fathers were sent back to their dioceses to carry out its renewal. Vatican II became the most influential event in Catholic life of the twentieth century.

sources.text: Vatican, Closing of the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council (1965) (vatican.va)

events.title: Luther burns the papal bull at Wittenberg
events.shortBlurb: Before a crowd outside Wittenberg, Martin Luther cast the papal bull threatening his excommunication into the flames, an open breach with Rome…
body: On 10 December 1520, at the Elster Gate of Wittenberg, Martin Luther publicly burned the bull Exsurge Domine, by which Pope Leo X had condemned forty-one propositions drawn from his writings and threatened him with excommunication unless he recanted within sixty days. Into the fire he also cast volumes of the canon law.

The gesture was an open and irrevocable rejection of papal authority. On 3 January 1521 Leo X excommunicated him by the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, and that spring Luther stood before the Diet of Worms; the Reformation had passed the point of return.

events.title: Pius XI proclaims the Feast of Christ the King
events.shortBlurb: In the Holy Year encyclical Quas Primas, Pope Pius XI instituted a new feast honoring the kingship of Christ over all peoples and nations…
body: On 11 December 1925 Pope Pius XI issued the encyclical Quas Primas and established the feast of Christ the King. Against the secularism and rising nationalism of the age, the pope taught that Christ holds a true kingship over individuals, families, and states — a reign of truth, justice, and peace to which even civil authority is subject.

The feast was first kept on the last Sunday of October; in the reform of the calendar after the Second Vatican Council it was moved to the last Sunday of the liturgical year, where it now crowns the Church's year.

sources.text: Vatican, Encyclical Quas Primas of Pope Pius XI (1925) (vatican.va)

events.title: The abdication of Pope Celestine V
events.shortBlurb: Five months after his election, the hermit-pope Celestine V renounced the papacy, the first pope to resign of his own free will…
body: On 13 December 1294 Pope Celestine V — the aged hermit Peter of Morrone, drawn from his mountain cell and elected pope only five months before — solemnly renounced the office he found himself unequal to govern. He is remembered as the first pope to abdicate freely, having first established by decree the pope's right to resign.

His successor, Boniface VIII, kept the old man in custody, where he died in 1296; he was canonized in 1313. Dante placed the shade of one who made the great refusal at the gate of his Inferno, an allusion many have read as pointing to Celestine.

events.title: The Council of Trent opens
events.shortBlurb: The great council of the Catholic Reformation began its work, defining doctrine and reforming discipline for centuries to come…
body: The Council of Trent opened on 13 December 1545 and, meeting in sessions over eighteen years, answered the doctrinal challenges of the Reformation and undertook a thorough reform of Church discipline. It clarified the teaching on Scripture and tradition, justification, the sacraments, and the Mass, and set in motion the seminaries and catechesis of the Catholic Reformation.
Its decrees shaped Catholic life until the twentieth century.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), General Church history

events.title: The Synod of Sutri
events.shortBlurb: A synod called by the German king Henry III swept away three rival claimants to the papacy and opened the era of reform…
body: On 20 December 1046, at Sutri north of Rome, a synod convened under King Henry III of Germany confronted the scandal of three men claiming the papacy at once — Benedict IX, Sylvester III, and Gregory VI. The synod deposed the rivals, and within days a reforming German bishop was elected as Pope Clement II, who then crowned Henry emperor.

Sutri broke the grip of the Roman noble factions on the papacy and prepared the way for the Gregorian Reform, the great eleventh-century movement to free the Church from lay control and to renew the life of the clergy.

events.title: The first recorded Christmas at Rome
events.shortBlurb: The oldest surviving record of the Church keeping the Nativity of Christ on 25 December points to the year 336 in the city of Rome…
body: The Chronograph of 354, a Roman almanac, preserves a calendar whose list of commemorations begins on 25 December with a note of the birth of Christ in Bethlehem of Judea. The entry reflects a usage already established by the year 336, the earliest firm evidence that the Roman Church celebrated the Lord's Nativity on that day.

From Rome the observance of 25 December spread through the West and, in time, much of the East, where 6 January had been the older feast of the Lord's manifestation. The choice of date was bound up both with ancient reckonings of the date of the Passion and with the turning of the sun after the winter solstice, Christ being hailed as the true Sun of Justice.

events.title: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne Emperor
events.shortBlurb: On Christmas Day in St. Peter’s, Pope Leo III set a crown on the head of the Frankish king Charlemagne and hailed him Emperor, binding the fortunes of the Papacy and the West…
body: During Mass on Christmas Day of the year 800, in the basilica of St. Peter at Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charles the Great, king of the Franks, as Emperor of the Romans, and the people acclaimed him.

The event marked the rise of a Christian empire in the West and set the pattern of relations between the Papacy and the emperors for centuries — a partnership, and often a struggle, at the heart of medieval Christendom.

events.title: St. Francis makes the crib at Greccio
events.shortBlurb: In a hillside cave at Greccio, St. Francis of Assisi arranged the first Christmas crèche, that the birth of the Lord might be seen with the eyes…
body: At Christmas of 1223, in the Italian village of Greccio, St. Francis of Assisi prepared a manger with hay and brought an ox and an ass to a cave in the hillside, so that the people might behold, as if with their own eyes, the poverty in which the Infant Christ was born at Bethlehem. Mass was offered over the manger, and Francis, who was a deacon, sang the Gospel and preached of the babe of Bethlehem.

His biographer Thomas of Celano records the wonder of that night, and from Greccio the custom of the Christmas crib spread through the whole Church, becoming one of the best-loved devotions of Christendom.

events.title: The dedication of Hagia Sophia
events.shortBlurb: The Emperor Justinian dedicated at Constantinople the great church of Holy Wisdom, the wonder of Christian architecture for a thousand years…
body: On 27 December 537 the Emperor Justinian I dedicated in Constantinople the rebuilt basilica of Hagia Sophia, the church of the Holy Wisdom, raised in less than six years by the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus after the earlier church was destroyed in the Nika riots. Its vast dome, seeming to hang from heaven, made it the marvel of the Christian world.

For nine centuries Hagia Sophia was the cathedral of the Byzantine emperors and the heart of Eastern Christendom; tradition reports that Justinian, entering the finished church, cried out that he had surpassed Solomon. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 it was turned into a mosque.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Thomas Becket
events.shortBlurb: In his own cathedral at Canterbury, the archbishop Thomas Becket was cut down by four knights of King Henry II…
body: On the evening of 29 December 1170, four knights of King Henry II of England, taking as license the king's angry words against his archbishop, entered Canterbury Cathedral and murdered Thomas Becket near the altar as the monks were singing Vespers. He had returned only weeks before from six years of exile, still defending the liberties of the Church against the crown.

Christendom was horrified; miracles were soon reported at his tomb, and Becket was canonized within three years, in 1173. Canterbury became one of the great pilgrim shrines of Europe until it was destroyed under King Henry VIII.
